lead: A living cell is a tiny battery. Its membrane separates charged ions, so the inside sits at a small negative voltage compared with the outside. This resting voltage is near −70 mV. When a stimulus pushes the voltage past a threshold, the cell fires a brief positive spike called an action potential. Every bioelectric recorder — ECG, EEG, EMG — measures these voltages after they have spread through tissue. The cell model explains why the signals exist, why they are small, and why they are brief. This is the electrophysiology behind every recorder.
prereq: You need: school-level idea of a cell membrane and ions, plus the units below; electrode theory is in electrode theory and amplification in bio-amplifiers.

blocks.text: Every cell is wrapped in a lipid membrane. The membrane is a thin insulator. Ion channels are selective pores. The main ions are Na+, K+, Cl− and large negatively charged proteins. The sodium-potassium pump uses energy from ATP to move three Na+ ions out and two K+ ions in for each cycle. This pump builds and maintains concentration gradients: Na+ is high outside, K+ is high inside.

At rest, K+ leak channels are more open than Na+ leak channels. K+ leaves down its gradient, carrying positive charge out. That makes the inside negative. Na+ leaks in and the pump removes it, so the gradients do not run down.

blocks.where: V<sub>m</sub> is membrane voltage; V<sub>inside</sub> is the voltage inside the cell; V<sub>outside</sub> is the voltage outside. A negative V<sub>m</sub> means the inside is negative with respect to the outside.

blocks.text: For one ion, the Nernst idea gives an equilibrium voltage: the voltage that would balance that ion's concentration difference. It depends on the log of the outside-to-inside concentration ratio. The Goldman idea combines several ions, weighted by how permeable the membrane is to each. At rest, K+ dominates, but some Na+ permeability makes the resting potential less negative than the K+ equilibrium voltage. In a typical neuron the resting potential is about −70 mV inside. Other cells differ.

sections.h3: Action potential: threshold, spike and reset

blocks.text: An action potential is a rapid change in V<sub>m</sub> that travels along a nerve or muscle fibre. It starts only when a stimulus depolarises the membrane to threshold. Threshold is a voltage, not a time; a common value is about −55 mV inside. Depolarisation means making V<sub>m</sub> less negative. A stimulus below threshold produces a small local change that dies away. At threshold, voltage-gated Na+ channels open.

Na+ enters, so V<sub>m</sub> rises quickly toward positive values. This is the depolarisation phase. The peak is often near +30 mV. At the peak, Na+ channels inactivate and voltage-gated K+ channels open. K+ leaves the cell, carrying positive charge out, so V<sub>m</sub> falls. This is repolarisation. K+ channels close slowly, so V<sub>m</sub> often goes below the resting value. That undershoot is hyperpolarisation. The pump and leak channels then restore the resting state.

After a spike the membrane has a refractory period. During the absolute refractory period no new action potential can start. During the relative refractory period a stronger-than-normal stimulus can start one. The action potential is all-or-none: once threshold is crossed, the height and shape are fixed for that cell. A stronger stimulus does not make a taller spike; it makes more spikes per second. This is why nerve signals carry information in timing and frequency.

A plot of V<sub>m</sub> against time shows rest as a flat line, a sharp rise at threshold, a peak, a fall and a small undershoot. The x-axis is time in milliseconds (ms); 1 ms = 0.001 s. The y-axis is membrane voltage in millivolts (mV); 1 mV = 0.001 V. A typical spike lasts 1–2 ms in a nerve, longer in some muscle cells.

The figure shows rest near −70 mV, threshold at −55 mV, peak at +30 mV, and return to rest. Notice that threshold is above rest: it is a depolarised value. The peak-to-peak amplitude from rest to peak is 100 mV, not 85 mV. Recorders do not see the cell directly. An electrode converts ionic current to electronic current (electrode theory), and a bio-amplifier raises the small differential voltage (bio-amplifiers). The ECG, EEG and EMG chapters apply this cell source at body-surface scale.

figure.caption: The trace shows one action potential: rest near −70 mV, threshold at −55 mV, peak at +30 mV, and return to rest. Notice that threshold is a depolarised value, not the resting value.

spec.aria: A plot of membrane voltage in millivolts against time in milliseconds, showing rest at -70 mV, threshold at -55 mV, peak at +30 mV, and return to rest.

examples.question: A neuron has resting potential −70 mV inside, threshold −55 mV inside, and peak +30 mV inside. (a) Find the depolarisation needed to reach threshold. (b) Find the peak-to-peak amplitude from resting potential to peak.
steps: Depolarisation to threshold is threshold minus resting voltage: (−55 mV) − (−70 mV) = 15 mV.
Peak-to-peak amplitude is peak minus resting voltage: (+30 mV) − (−70 mV) = 100 mV.
The two minus signs in each subtraction matter: subtracting a negative voltage adds its magnitude.
examples.answer: The depolarisation needed is 15 mV, and the peak-to-peak amplitude from rest to peak is 100 mV.
examples.check:
rest = -70
threshold = -55
peak = 30
depolarisation = threshold - rest
amplitude = peak - rest
print(depolarisation)
print(amplitude)

traps: Sign slip: resting potential is negative inside; writing +70 mV reverses the cell.
Threshold is a depolarised voltage near −55 mV, not the resting voltage; a stimulus below threshold does not fire.
All-or-none: a stronger stimulus increases firing rate, not spike height.
Unit slip: mV and ms are thousandths; 100 mV = 0.1 V, and 2 ms = 0.002 s.
Peak-to-peak amplitude is peak minus rest, not peak minus threshold.

quiz.q: Define resting potential and state a typical value for a neuron.
quiz.a: Resting potential is the membrane voltage of a cell at rest, inside with respect to outside. A typical neuron value is about −70 mV.

quiz.q: Why is the resting potential negative inside the cell?
quiz.a: K+ leak channels let K+ leave, carrying positive charge out. The sodium-potassium pump moves three Na+ out and two K+ in, and Na+ leak is small. The result is a negative inside voltage.

quiz.q: A cell has resting potential −70 mV, threshold −50 mV and peak +20 mV. Find the depolarisation to threshold and the peak-to-peak amplitude from rest to peak.
Why does a stronger stimulus not make a taller action potential?
quiz.a: The action potential is all-or-none. Once threshold is crossed, channel gates and ion gradients set the spike height. A stronger stimulus starts more spikes per second, not a bigger spike.
It is the time after an action potential when a new action potential is hard or impossible to start. Absolute means none can start; relative means a stronger stimulus can start one.

quiz.q: If resting potential is −75 mV and threshold is −60 mV, what depolarisation is needed to reach threshold?

beyond: Not for the exam. Patch-clamp amplifiers record single ion channels, and cardiac and neural drug tests use the same resting and action potential ideas. Wearable biopotential systems push electrodes and amplifiers toward low power and dry contact. Search next for patch clamp, voltage clamp, Hodgkin-Huxley model, and cardiac action potential. The Hodgkin-Huxley model describes channel conductances with differential equations.
